---
title: "Module 1 — Windows & Acquisition"
subtitle: "The four standard cardiac windows, machine setup, and normal anatomy"
---

## 1. Overview

Bedside cardiac ultrasound begins with four standard windows. Each window shows the heart from a different acoustic angle, and each reveals structures that the others cannot. No single window is sufficient for a complete exam — the goal is to build a three-dimensional mental model of the heart by integrating what you see across all four views.

This module covers:

- Machine setup and probe selection
- How to obtain each window reliably
- The normal anatomy visible in each view
- Common normal variants and pitfalls

Pathology is introduced in later modules. The goal here is to recognize a normal study confidently before encountering abnormalities.

---

## 2. Machine setup

*Before placing the probe, set the machine correctly.*

**Probe:** Phased array (cardiac) probe. The small footprint fits between ribs; the sector beam provides the wide near-field needed to visualize the full heart. A curvilinear probe is an acceptable substitute when a phased array is unavailable.

**Preset:** Select the **cardiac preset**. This does two important things:
1. Inverts the depth convention so the apex appears at the top of the screen in apical views (cardiac orientation).
2. Optimizes gain, frequency, and frame rate for cardiac imaging.

**Depth:** Adjust so the far wall of the structure of interest is visible with a small margin beyond it. A common error is too little depth, which clips posterior structures. A second common error is too much depth, which makes cardiac structures appear small and reduces resolution.

**Gain:** Adjust overall gain so that blood appears dark (anechoic) and myocardium appears mid-gray. Overgained images obscure the distinction between fluid and tissue.

**Indicator convention:** In cardiac imaging, the probe indicator is displayed on the **right side of the screen**. Confirm this on your machine before starting — some machines default to the left (radiology convention). If the indicator displays on the wrong side, the image will appear mirrored.

---

## 3. The four standard windows

---

### Subcostal four-chamber view

::: {.callout-tip}
**Video slot:** Subcostal four-chamber acquisition — probe position, indicator orientation, fanning technique, optimization in a difficult patient.
:::

**Probe placement:** Subxiphoid, probe nearly flat against the abdomen (15–20° angle above horizontal). Indicator points to the patient's **left**. Use the left lobe of the liver as an acoustic window — it transmits sound better than air-filled structures.

**How to optimize:**
- Ask the patient to inhale slowly and hold — this drops the diaphragm, bringing the heart into the imaging plane.
- Apply firm, steady pressure. Do not jab — sustained pressure displaces bowel gas and improves the window.
- If the view is poor, try moving the probe slightly to the patient's right (more liver), or ask the patient to bend their knees to relax the abdominal wall.
- In intubated patients, this window is often the most accessible — it does not require repositioning.

**Normal anatomy visible:**

| Structure | Location in image |
|---|---|
| Right ventricle | Nearest the probe (top of image) |
| Interventricular septum | Separates RV and LV |
| Left ventricle | Deep to the septum |
| Right atrium | Upper right |
| Left atrium | Deepest chamber |
| Tricuspid valve | Between RA and RV |
| Mitral valve | Between LA and LV |
| Pericardium | Bright echogenic line surrounding the heart |
| Liver | Near-field acoustic window (top left) |

**Why this window first:** In undifferentiated shock or cardiac arrest, the subcostal view is the fastest and does not require repositioning the patient. In a supine, ventilated patient, it is often the only window achievable.

---

### Parasternal long axis

::: {.callout-tip}
**Video slot:** Parasternal long axis acquisition — rib interspace selection, indicator toward the right shoulder, tilting to optimize the LV long axis.
:::

**Probe placement:** Left parasternal border, **3rd or 4th intercostal space**, indicator pointing toward the patient's **right shoulder** (approximately 10–11 o'clock). The imaging plane cuts through the long axis of the left ventricle.

**How to optimize:**
- Move up or down one interspace if the LV appears foreshortened or the apex is cut off.
- Tilt the probe slightly medially or laterally to bring the aortic root and LV apex into the same plane.
- The aortic valve should appear central, opening symmetrically in systole.
- The LV walls should appear equal in thickness and the LV should not be foreshortened.

**Normal anatomy visible:**

| Structure | Location in image |
|---|---|
| Right ventricle | Near-field, anterior (top of image) |
| Interventricular septum | Separates RV and LV |
| Left ventricle | Central, posterior to septum |
| Anterior mitral leaflet | Long, swings widely open in diastole |
| Posterior mitral leaflet | Short, moves oppositely |
| Left atrium | Posterior, deep |
| Aortic valve | Right side of image, 3 thin leaflets |
| Aortic root / LVOT | Connects LV to aortic valve |
| Descending thoracic aorta | Far left, appears as a round cross-section |

**Key landmark:** The descending thoracic aorta appears in cross-section at the far left of the image. This landmark is used to distinguish pericardial fluid (anterior to the aorta) from pleural fluid (posterior to the aorta) — covered in Module 4.

---

### Parasternal short axis

::: {.callout-tip}
**Video slots:**
- PSAX at the aortic valve level — the "Mercedes-Benz" sign, right ventricular outflow tract, pulmonary valve
- PSAX at the mitral valve level — the "fish mouth" opening of the mitral valve
- PSAX at the papillary muscle level — the "donut" view, concentric LV contraction, papillary muscles
:::

**Probe placement:** Same position as PLAX (left parasternal border, 3rd or 4th ICS), then **rotate the probe 90° clockwise** (indicator moves to the patient's left shoulder, approximately 1–2 o'clock). The imaging plane now cuts the heart in cross-section.

**How to obtain different levels:** Fan the probe from the base (toward the right shoulder) to the apex (toward the left hip) to image successively lower cross-sections of the heart.

**How to optimize:**
- The LV should appear round (not elliptical) in cross-section at the papillary muscle level. If oval, the plane is slightly oblique — adjust.
- At the aortic valve level, all three cusps should be visible forming a Y-shape (Mercedes-Benz) on closure.

**Normal anatomy by level:**

*Aortic valve level (most basal):*

| Structure | Location |
|---|---|
| Aortic valve | Central — three cusps (right, left, non-coronary) |
| Right ventricular outflow tract | Anterior, wraps around the aorta |
| Pulmonary valve | Anterior left |
| Tricuspid valve | Right |
| Right atrium | Right |
| Left atrium | Posterior |

*Mitral valve level:*

| Structure | Location |
|---|---|
| Left ventricle | Central, with the mitral valve visible as a "fish mouth" opening in diastole |
| Right ventricle | Anterior, crescent-shaped |
| Anterior mitral leaflet | Anterior (longer) |
| Posterior mitral leaflet | Posterior (shorter) |

*Papillary muscle level (mid-ventricular):*

| Structure | Location |
|---|---|
| Left ventricle | Round, central — the "donut" view |
| Right ventricle | Crescent-shaped, anterior |
| Interventricular septum | Separates RV and LV |
| Anterolateral papillary muscle | Left lateral wall |
| Posteromedial papillary muscle | Inferior wall |

**Why this window matters:** PSAX at the papillary muscle level is the best single view for a quick visual EF estimate (does the LV nearly obliterate in systole?) and for identifying the D-sign (septal flattening from RV pressure or volume overload — Module 3).

---

### Apical four-chamber

::: {.callout-tip}
**Video slot:** Apical four-chamber acquisition — finding the PMI, lateral decubitus positioning, depth adjustment to bring the apex to the top of the screen.
:::

**Probe placement:** Point of maximal impulse (PMI), typically **5th intercostal space, midclavicular line**. Indicator points to the patient's **left** (3 o'clock position). The imaging plane cuts the heart from the apex downward, showing all four chambers simultaneously.

**How to optimize:**
- Left lateral decubitus positioning brings the heart toward the chest wall and significantly improves image quality. Use this position whenever possible.
- In the cardiac preset, the apex should appear at the **top** of the screen. Adjust depth so the apex is at the top with a small margin.
- In obese patients or those with COPD, the PMI may be displaced laterally or inferiorly — palpate for it rather than assuming position.
- If the view is suboptimal, try moving one interspace lateral or inferior.

**Normal anatomy visible:**

| Structure | Location in image |
|---|---|
| Left ventricular apex | Top center |
| Left ventricle | Left side of image |
| Right ventricle | Right side of image (normally smaller) |
| Mitral valve | Left AV valve — opens widely in diastole |
| Tricuspid valve | Right AV valve — inserts slightly more apically than mitral |
| Left atrium | Left, posterior (bottom left) |
| Right atrium | Right, posterior (bottom right) |
| Interventricular septum | Vertical, separates LV and RV |
| Interatrial septum | Thin membrane between LA and RA |

**Key observation:** The tricuspid valve inserts slightly more apically on the septum than the mitral valve — this normal offsetting helps identify which AV valve is which. If a structure appears to insert on the right side of the septum closer to the apex, it is the tricuspid valve and the chamber to its right is the RV.

---

## 4. Normal anatomy and normal variants

*The library of normal studies.*

Fellows need to see many normal studies before pathology becomes recognizable. The section below describes what a normal heart looks like in each window and identifies the most common normal variants that may be mistaken for pathology.

::: {.callout-tip}
**Video slots:** Normal studies across body habitus — thin patient, obese patient, COPD, post-CABG. Aim to review at least 10 normal loops in each window before moving to pathology modules.
:::

### Normal LV size and wall thickness

- **LV internal diameter (diastole):** 3.8–5.5 cm (PLAX, M-mode or 2D)
- **Interventricular septum thickness:** 0.6–1.1 cm
- **Posterior wall thickness:** 0.6–1.1 cm
- **LV wall motion:** Symmetric, brisk inward thickening in systole

### Normal RV size

On apical four-chamber, the RV occupies approximately the right one-third of the image and is clearly smaller than the LV. A rough rule: the RV should appear no larger than two-thirds the size of the LV. The RV free wall is thin and contracts vigorously.

### Normal valve motion

- **Aortic valve:** Three thin leaflets opening to the aortic walls in systole; central coaptation in diastole. On PSAX: Y-shaped (Mercedes-Benz) closure pattern.
- **Mitral valve:** Anterior leaflet swings widely open in diastole ("fish mouth" on PSAX). Posterior leaflet moves oppositely and is shorter. Both coapt in systole with no gap.
- **Tricuspid valve:** Three thin leaflets, not always individually distinguishable. Visible in subcostal and apical views.

### Normal pericardium

A thin, bright (hyperechoic) line surrounding the heart on all views. It moves with the heart. No echo-free space should be visible between the visceral (inner) and pericardial (outer) layers. Covered in detail in Module 4.

### Normal variants

**Pericardial fat pad:** An echogenic (not anechoic) structure anterior to the RV, most prominent on subcostal and PLAX views. Common in older and obese patients. Does not shift with repositioning. Distinguished from pericardial effusion by its echogenicity — fat is bright, effusion is black.

**Epicardial fat:** A thin echogenic layer between the myocardium and visceral pericardium, most prominent over the RV free wall and in the AV groove. Moves with the heart. More prominent in obese patients.

**Moderator band:** A muscular structure crossing the RV cavity from the interventricular septum to the anterior free wall — most visible on apical four-chamber. Normal structure; should not be mistaken for a mass or thrombus.

**False tendons:** Thin echogenic linear structures traversing the LV cavity, usually from wall to wall. Normal variant; can be mistaken for vegetations or thrombus. They are fixed, linear, and do not move independently.

**Trabeculations:** Muscular ridges along the inner LV wall, most prominent at the apex. Normal. Prominent apical trabeculations may raise the question of non-compaction cardiomyopathy — if extensive and bilateral, refer for formal echo.

**Chiari network:** A fenestrated, mobile structure in the right atrium near the inferior vena cava — a remnant of the embryologic valve of the sinus venosus. Normal; may be mistaken for a thrombus or vegetation.

## 5. Quiz

Anki deck for spaced repetition: *link coming soon.*

::: {.callout-note}
**Q1.** The probe is placed at the left parasternal border with the indicator pointing toward the right shoulder. Which window are you in, and which structures should be visible?

::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"}
**Answer**
Parasternal long axis (PLAX). Structures visible: right ventricle (near-field), interventricular septum, left ventricle, anterior and posterior mitral valve leaflets, left atrium, aortic valve, aortic root/LVOT, and the descending thoracic aorta in cross-section at the far left.
:::

**Q2.** Starting from the PLAX position, you rotate the probe 90° clockwise. What window have you moved into, and what does the LV look like at the papillary muscle level?

::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"}
**Answer**
Parasternal short axis (PSAX). At the papillary muscle level, the LV appears as a round structure in cross-section — the "donut" view. The RV appears as a crescent anteriorly. The anterolateral and posteromedial papillary muscles are visible as two echogenic nodules on the LV wall. The LV should contract concentrically and symmetrically, nearly obliterating in systole.
:::

**Q3.** In the subcostal four-chamber view, which chamber is closest to the probe, and why does this matter clinically?

::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"}
**Answer**
The right ventricle is closest to the probe (nearest the transducer). This matters because the subcostal view is often the first obtained in an unstable patient, and the RV free wall is the first structure encountered. RV dilation, chamber collapse in tamponade, and pericardial effusion (which separates the heart from the pericardium) are all visible at this near-field position.
:::

**Q4.** You are in the apical four-chamber view. How do you distinguish the mitral valve from the tricuspid valve?

::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"}
**Answer**
The tricuspid valve inserts slightly more apically on the interventricular septum than the mitral valve. On the apical four-chamber, the tricuspid is on the right side of the image (associated with the RV and RA), and its septal leaflet attaches closer to the apex. The mitral valve is on the left side of the image. This apical offset is a reliable distinguishing feature.
:::

**Q5.** At the aortic valve level on PSAX, you see only two leaflets forming an oval "fish mouth" instead of the expected three-leaflet Mercedes-Benz pattern. What is the most likely explanation?

::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"}
**Answer**
Bicuspid aortic valve — a congenital variant in which the aortic valve has two leaflets instead of three, often with a raphe (a vestigial ridge where two cusps fused). It is the most common congenital cardiac abnormality (~1–2% of the population) and is associated with aortic stenosis, aortic regurgitation, and aortopathy. The patient should be referred for formal echo to assess valve function and aortic root diameter.
:::

**Q6.** You see a bright, linear structure crossing the LV cavity from wall to wall on apical four-chamber. It does not move independently. What is it, and do you need to act on it?

::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"}
**Answer**
A false tendon (aberrant chordae tendineae). These are normal variants — thin, linear, fixed echogenic structures crossing the LV cavity, usually without hemodynamic significance. They should not be mistaken for vegetations (which are mobile, irregular, and attached to valve leaflets) or thrombus (which is usually located at the apex and has a different morphology). No action needed.
:::

**Q7.** What is the correct indicator orientation for each of the four standard cardiac windows?

::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"}
**Answer**
- **Subcostal four-chamber:** Indicator to the patient's left
- **Parasternal long axis:** Indicator toward the patient's right shoulder (~10–11 o'clock)
- **Parasternal short axis:** Indicator toward the patient's left shoulder (~1–2 o'clock)
- **Apical four-chamber:** Indicator to the patient's left (3 o'clock)
:::
:::
